passed, because a name's wrapping and a page's height are the *serif's*
business and the serif had been left alone. The runner's fallback serif is
**narrower** than Literata, so the rehearsal has to push both ways at once:
Verdana for the utility face, wider than DejaVu; Times New Roman for the serif,
narrower than Literata.

With both forced, all three come back on this desk **with the runner's own
numbers**:

| | CI | the rehearsal, here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily scroll | expected 1500, received **1399** | expected 1500, received **1399** |
| facet chips | expected 1 line, received **2** | expected 1 line, received **2** |
| Macarius the New | expected 3 lines, received **2** | expected 3 lines, received **2** |

A rehearsal that only half-applies is the more dangerous artefact, because it
is green for the wrong reason — which is why the measurement is printed on
every run and not only on a failure. `[facet row, native utility face] column
580 px, needs 604.2, 2 line(s), face Verdana` is the harness saying it bit.

The peer session drew the boundary that prompted this: it ran the rehearsal
itself and reported it green, and then said plainly that it could **not**
reproduce the old red, because the pre-fix spec predates fixtures.js and never
imported the harness. That was the right thing to say and the right gap to
name — CI's red had been standing in for a back-out that had not been done.

### And then the clock rolled over, and took three more

The full gate ran green at 510 and then, at midnight, went red on three tests
that no one had touched — the same class again, in its other form. **Today is
not a constant either.**

* `the rail scrolls in one piece` compared the day beyond the strip's trailing
  edge against **the 28th**, and the clock reached the 28th. A rail day carries
  no class of its own; `markRail` adds `is-today` and nothing else, so the
  comparison had been `'' === ''` until the moment one of the two days became
  today. It compares against whichever day in the strip *is* ordinary now —
  not today, not selected — which is a property rather than a date.
* Two scroll tests wanted a tall Daily page, and **today's had almost nothing
  in it**: 1127 px against the 2605 the test was written on. Not a fault —
  the corpus's saints run out before its liturgical records do, so 28 August
  drew readings, hymns and a fast with no hero and an empty register, which is
  the designed empty-day state. Both now take their depth from the page, and
  the Daily-return test uses a 400 px window so there is something below the
  fold to scroll on a day that holds little. The Daily nav goes to `/`, which
  is today by definition, so neither test can simply pick a fuller day.

Three traps, one shape: **a number that came from this machine.** Its face, its
clock, its calendar's contents. The remedy is the same each time — take the
number from the page, or pin the condition that produces it.

### Verification

**171 unit, 510 browser** at the full gate, both projects, Playwright's exit
code read directly. The rehearsal green across all five specs at desktop — 254
passed, one documented opt-out — and red on all three font assertions when they
are backed out to their committed form, matching CI number for number. Four
packs 338 of 338. The three clock failures were fixed after that gate and
verified green on their own; no `src/` file changed with them.

## Amendment 59 — fifteen refinements, and a native drag nobody asked for (2026-08-28, eighteenth sitting)

Fifteen instructions in one message. Most are small; three are not, and one of
the small ones turned out to be a bug in the browser's own behaviour that had
been sitting under the carousel since the row was built.

### The carousel

* **The card follows the window's height, not only its width** ("the saint
  images in the carousel stay the same width which is good in full screen BUT
  not good when window is resized"). `--cx-w` is `clamp(150px, 30vh, 240px)` on
  a desk: 30vh reaches the old 240 at about an 800 px window and holds there, so
  a full screen is exactly what it was, and a 560 px window gets a smaller card
  rather than one whose caption is below the fold. A clamp rather than a second
  breakpoint, because what changed is continuous.

* **A press no longer stops the row for good** ("If you click a second time,
  the auto scroll stops completely? … It seems like the auto scroll can get
  reset by pressing the Advanced search button and then back to the Carousel
  mode"). That last clause is the diagnosis, and it was the author's. The track
  is `tabindex="0"`, so any press focuses it; `focused` latched until focus went
  somewhere else, which a second press on the same row never does. The only
  thing that cleared it was the mode toggle, because leaving the carousel
  destroys the loop and coming back builds a fresh one.

  Focus is split by how it arrived now. **Keyboard focus still holds the row** —
  a reader tabbing through cards cannot be chasing them — and a pointer press
  holds it for two and a half seconds and lets go.

* **And the wheel works while it is held** ("if you click and then instantly try
  to scroll, it cant scroll. You have to wait"). One test governed both the
  drift and the wheel: the frame returned early when the row was held, and the
  early return zeroed `wheelVel` before it could be spent. Stopping the drift
  and refusing the reader's own scroll are not the same thing and no longer
  share a test — `frozen()` is *no writes at all*, `drifting()` is only whether
  the row moves by itself.

* **Hold and drag with the mouse**, which is where the sitting's one genuine
  browser-behaviour bug was. Every card is an `<a>` around an `<img>`, and both
  are natively draggable: pressing one and moving started Chromium's own
  link-and-image drag, which takes the pointer into a nested loop and hands the
  reader a ghost of the icon instead of moving the row. **A harness driving the
  same gesture hangs outright**, which is how it was found — the test did not
  fail, it stopped, twice, and a probe printed `down` and nothing after it.
  `dragstart` is refused on the track. There was never anything on this row
  worth dragging out of it.

* **A phone pairs the wide icons and spreads the row vertically** ("double stack
  any saint images and texts that are wide aspect ratio, and arrange them a bit
  more spread out vertically, not all lined up at the bottom").

  A track child is a **cell** now — one tall saint, or two wide ones sharing a
  column. That wrapper is the whole trick: `loopScroll` works out its period
  from the offset between child `buffer` and child `buffer + count`, so two
  saints inside one child leaves the arithmetic untouched. A two-row grid over
  the track itself would have packed each period from wherever the last one
  ended, and a period starting mid-column packs differently from one starting at
  a column edge — a drift the wrap cannot correct.

  The first build paired *neighbours*, and produced one pair: 44 of the corpus's
  128 icons are wide but scattered, so adjacency in a shuffled pool of 48 is
  rare. Pairing them deliberately gets thirteen. The three lift classes are the
  spread, dealt from the cell's place in the run rather than its place in the
  rendered strip — a card and its clones must rest at the same height or the
  wrap becomes visible, which is the one thing it exists to hide.

* **A finger under the row scrolls the page** ("if your hand accidentally
  touches the space under the carousel, the scroll instantly stops"). `pan-x`
  alone told the browser that a touch starting anywhere on the track pans
  horizontally *and nothing else* — including the padding under the cards, which
  looks like page and is not. `pan-x pan-y` costs the row nothing, because it
  scrolls only on x.

### The stamp

**The name is a mark rather than a word** ("make sure this new website title is
applied to all languages, it no longer gets translated, it stays constant as a
stamp of branding"). `BRAND` in ui/strings.js is what the masthead, the veil and
the tab print in every pack. `site.name` and `tabName` stay in all five packs so
the coverage script has one key set, and because a translated name is a decision
a future author might want back — but **nothing reads them**, and the comment
there says so, because a key that looks live and is not is worse than no key.

The gap between the two words is a space set at **half the font size**, which is
half a space wide, because a glyph's advance scales with the size. No em-guess
at what a space measures in a face that is Nicefore once it loads and Literata
until it does.

**And the face is `swap`, alone among this project's faces** ("Sometimes on
mobile, the title does not render in the new font, but in the old font"). That
is `font-display: optional` keeping its promise: a few frames for the file, and
if the network has not answered, the fallback *for the life of the page*. A
phone on a slow connection got Literata in the masthead permanently and a warm
reload got the stamp — two mastheads for one reader, which is the one thing a
brand cannot be. Everything else here stays `optional` and should: that policy
protects a page of prose from reflowing, and the masthead is two words in a
fixed box.

The `html[lang='en']` scoping went with it. It existed because the other packs
printed their own accented names, which this Latin-and-Greek-caps face cannot
set; there are no other names now.

### All Saints

* **Every calendar is ticked** ("display all saints by default … so that people
  get exposed to the full range and not have hidden saints without their
  realising. Orthodoxy allows for personal freedom in private prayer life"). It
  opened on the header's own calendar, which showed a reader who had chosen
  Russian 426 of the 742 and never said the other 316 were there. The header
  still decides what the *Daily* page reckons by.

  The facet's options are read from the DOM rather than from the church list, so
  whatever it is offering is what gets ticked. **`Not calendarised` is
  implemented and does not render**: all 742 carry a venerated attestation, so
  the option would select nobody. The predicate exists — a saint arriving
  without a calendar would otherwise be silently unreachable from this page,
  which is the failure the instruction is about — and the option appears the day
  the corpus has someone to put in it.

* **The denominator recedes** ("make the '/742' … a considerably darker /
  lighter … font colour so the main number that stands out is the number listed
  by the current filters"). Wrapped as a substring rather than given a second
  template, because all five packs write the ratio `{shown}/{total}`; the text
  is escaped first and the span added after, so the wrapping cannot smuggle
  markup out of a translation.

* **A random deal leads with pictures** ("make it so the first and third entries
  in the Advanced search are always profiles with an image"). Only under Random,
  because the other three orders are answers to a question the reader asked. The
  saint drawn up is any imaged one not already holding a showcase place —
  including one *above* it, which the first version missed: both pictures
  landing in the first two seats left nothing below the third to draw up, and
  the fixture caught it.

* **No mark on a card**, a day after the rows lost theirs, and with it the 40 px
  an imageless card's name and dates reserved for it. The gap between the name
  and the dates is the row's 2 px now rather than the card's 6 — "match the row
  view cards in terms of margins between name, subtext and frame", and the
  padding was already the same on both. `CARD_TEXT_HEIGHT` moved 92 → 88 with
  it, because a virtualised card's text block is a number in grid.js before it
  is a box in index.css.

* **No mark on a Continue reading row** either, which was the last row still
  wearing one. The author also asked why it was on the left: the row builds
  image, body, tools, and the Index's rows were re-ordered to name-first with
  the picture trailing while this one was not, so the mark sat where the dress
  it was copying had moved on from.

  **A note for whoever picks this up**: the shelf now has no Save control at
  all. The Saved shelf's own rows never had one and are rendered without
  `removable`, so nothing on that page un-saves a saint. That is consistent with
  where the author sent Save — "If people want to bookmark they can go to the
  profile page itself" — and it is stated here rather than discovered.

  It also corrects something said to the author on 2026-08-27: the claim that
  the shelf's mark "is the only un-save" was wrong. It was the *reading* row's
  mark, and the Saved shelf never had one.

### An icon, and the size of what is left

**Phanourios has his icon** — the author supplied the link. The licence, the
artist and the photographer's credit are as the Commons API answers for that
file rather than as read off a page, and it was fetched through
`Special:FilePath`, the file's own redirect, because a hotlinked thumbnail URL
is refused outright. 129 of 742 now carry a picture.

The instruction was larger than one saint: "Make sure all main saint cards for
each day and each calendar has an image in its profile." Measured over the days
the four calendars cover:

| | days | leading with no icon |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Russian | 36 | 10 |
| Greek | 36 | 11 |
| Serbian | 27 | 8 |
| Romanian | 34 | 9 |

**38 of 133**, and eleven of them are orderings rather than gaps: `pickHero` now
prefers an imaged saint *inside the sung pool*, which takes it to 27. That does
not reverse the author's own rule from 2026-08-22 — the saint a church sings for
is still the day's principal commemoration, ahead of any imaged saint it does
not sing for — it only decides which of the sung leads, where before that was
the date's hash alone.

The remaining 27 are days where nobody the church sings for has a picture, and
**19 distinct saints** among them have no icon anywhere on their day. Those need
licensed pictures, one at a time, which is a data job and this repository's
oldest rule about it stands: images are never bulk-fetched, and a licence is
something someone checked.

### What fifteen instructions cost the suite

Nineteen tests went red, every one a stale expectation rather than a fault, and
the shape is worth naming because it repeats: **an instruction that changes a
default breaks the tests that used that default as a fixture.**

Six ticked one calendar to make a filtered state, which is now a tick on a box
that is already ticked. They narrow by *unticking* through a new `onlyCalendar`
helper, so the next change to that default is one edit rather than six. Three
asserted a translated site name. Two asserted per-calendar counts through the
header, which no longer narrows this page — those keep the arithmetic and assert
it through the facet that does. Two more read the corpus's most recent saint,
which changed the moment the corpus stopped being one calendar's.

**Three tests lost their subject outright.** `the bookmark stands in the card
corner` and `a card lifespan stops before the bookmark` are about a mark that no
longer exists on a card, and there is nothing to re-point them at; what survives
of the second is already asserted by `a card lifespan is one line`. They are
removed rather than left as commented-out ballast. `there is one bookmark
drawing` moved to the saint's own page — its third home in five days, and the
last one available.

And **one rule in base.css is now dead**: the drop shadow that made a mark
legible over an icon matches nothing, because no mark on this site sits over a
picture any more. It is recorded where it stood rather than deleted in silence,
because the reasoning is sound and it is what should be reached for the day a
mark goes back over an icon.

One more correction, and it is one this session owed the author. On 2026-08-27
the shelf's mark was defended as "the only un-save" for the Saved list. It was
not: that mark was on the **Continue reading** rows, and the Saved shelf's own
rows are built by another function and never had one. So the control that was
argued for was never on the list it was argued for. After this instruction the
shelf has no un-save at all, and `saving persists across a reload` now says so
in as many words.

### Verification

**174 unit, 532 browser** across both projects. Eleven new browser tests, each
run at both widths. The four carousel behaviours were backed out together and
confirmed red before being restored, because a test for a drift that resumes can
pass against a row that never stopped.

Four packs 338 of 338 with no English fallbacks, and one new key —
`saints.filters.uncalendared` — translated in all five rather than left to fall
back, even though nothing renders it yet.

## Amendment 60 — the flakes were never the assertions (2026-08-28, nineteenth sitting)

Two items off HANDOFF's "needs the author" list, both decided by the author:
make the two known flakes deterministic rather than retried, and give
Athanasius the hierarch's reading.

### A flake in the rehearsal costs more than a flake in the gate

The rail's coast failed again that afternoon — inside the **COLD_FACE
rehearsal**, which is the run whose whole value is telling you whether CI will
be red. The peer session had to spend a run establishing that a commit was safe,
and the answer had nothing to do with the commit. Noise in the gate is a re-run;
noise in the instrument is a loss of the signal everything else now leans on.

### The assertions were the symptom

Both tests were rewritten first in the obvious way: stop sampling at a fixed
moment, wait for the state. `a thrown rail coasts` polled for the movement and
for two reads that agree instead of `waitForTimeout(150)` and
`waitForTimeout(1500)`; `the Index opens shuffled` waited for three cards to be
mounted before reading three names off a virtualised grid.

That took the rail from failing about once a suite to **1 in 32** — and the
remaining failure was the same numbers the peer had reported, 3527 against a
required 3547, with the poll running its full four seconds. The coast had not
been slow. **There had been no coast at all.**

### The gesture was never a flick

`up` in views/daily/picker.js reads the release velocity from the samples of the
last **120 ms**, and coasts only past `MIN_FLICK`. Driven through the harness's
mouse, every move is a separate round trip: under parallel load six of them
stretch past that window, the fresh samples collapse to one, `dt` is 0, the
velocity is 0, and the rail *settles*. Nothing was ever wrong with the rail. The
test had been asking for a coast without delivering a throw, and it was the
machine's load that decided which.

`throwRail` in e2e/helpers.js dispatches the gesture inside the page: four
pointermoves, 25 px apart, spaced by a **spin on `performance.now()`** rather
than by `setTimeout`, because a spin blocks and the spacing is therefore real
elapsed time whatever else the machine is doing. A 24 ms window well inside the
rail's 120, and the same velocity on every machine. The product path is
untouched — pointerdown, moves, pointerup, and the rail's own sampling decides.

**148 contended runs, zero failures**, at ten workers and under the rehearsal.

### And the test on the other side of it proved nothing at all

`under reduced motion a throw does not coast` used the same harness gesture, and
its assertion was the position 100 ms after release against the position 500 ms
after. **Backing the reduced-motion guard out of picker.js left it green.** The
coast is spent well inside the first 100 ms, so both samples were taken after
everything had already happened; it was reading the end of the story twice. Two
independent ways of saying nothing, in a test whose subject is an *absence*.

It watches for the coast now: `is-coasting` is on the strip for exactly as long
as one runs, so a MutationObserver armed before the flick either sees it or the
coast did not happen. Backed out again with that in place, it fails by name.

**The house rule found this, and only because it was applied to a test that was
already green.** A back-out is not a formality for a fix you are confident in —
it is the only thing that distinguishes a passing test from a watching one.

### Athanasius reads as a hierarch

Author: "do hierarch for athanasius." His record carried `bishop, theologian,
confessor`, and `confessor` is a rank in the precedence walk while the
hierarchical types are not — they fall through to the `honorific` fallback *on
purpose*, because "St" is how both major English calendars print a hierarch and
lib/honorific.js argues it at length. So the page about the archbishop who wrote
against the Arians announced him as a Confessor.

The code was doing what it was told: the word came out of his types, nothing in
the walk changed, and he reads **St Athanasius of Alexandria** with *Bishop,
Theologian* and *Hierarch* on the line below.

**Seven other records carry the same pair and are deliberately left alone.**
Barses and Eulogius of Edessa, Liberius of Rome, Martin the Pope, Nicholas of
Alma-Ata, Paul the New of Constantinople, Protogenes of Carrhae. For several of
them *Confessor* is the epithet the calendars actually print — Martin the
Confessor, Nicholas the Confessor — so the collision is only wrong where the
tradition says it is. That is a judgement per saint and the author's to make;
the count is in HANDOFF rather than acted on.

### Verification

**174 unit, 528 browser** across both projects. The two flakes verified against
a *rate* rather than a green — 148 contended runs at ten workers, under
COLD_FACE, with none failing — and both of the coast's claims backed out and
confirmed red: the coast removed, and the reduced-motion guard removed.

## Amendment 61 — a preload, and four things settled without code (2026-08-28, twentieth sitting)

### The two Latin subsets are preloaded

Addendum G6, decided by the author: "ignore svg, just preload texts as
recommended". An SVG wordmark was the alternative and is rejected, so GFS
Nicefore stays a face.

`font-display: optional` stands, and is the reason the preload is worth having
rather than an alternative to it: optional gives the file about a hundred
milliseconds and then keeps the fallback **for the life of the page**, so on a
cold load a reader gets Literata or does not, and later arrival changes nothing.
A preload starts the request with the HTML instead of after the stylesheet has
been parsed and matched. That is what puts the face inside the window on most
loads, with none of the shift `swap` would cost — and DESIGN.md's order stands:
zero shift outranks brand. This buys the brand back only where it is free.

**Two, not four.** `normal-latin` is the face every page is set in;
`normal-latin-ext` is not a luxury beside it, because the corpus is full of
names like *Cyriacus of Tazlău* whose accented characters live there, and a page
given one without the other changes face mid-word. Italic stays unpreloaded: it
belongs to lives and quotations rather than to first paint.

It is a Vite plugin because the filenames are hashed and cannot be written down.
**And the first build of it shipped the same subset twice.** Vite's hash can
itself begin with a hyphen — `literata-normal-latin-ext--vWOuwpV.woff2` — so a
pattern loose enough to match a hash after `literata-normal-latin-` also matches
`ext-`, and the plain Latin file was never found. It asks the bundle which
source each asset came from now. The test asserts the two hrefs *differ*, which
is the assertion that would have caught it, and that neither the italics nor the
Greek and Cyrillic subsets are preloaded, because the budget is the point.

### The non-civil reckoning was already there

Author: "yes add to saint page wherever the saint is on serbian or russian
calendar which use julian" — the *saint* page, not the Daily page, which has
been declined twice and is not reopened here.

**Nothing was built, because nothing was missing.** `formatFeast` in
data/calendars.js has printed a feast in its own reckoning all along, and the
saint page prints it beside the civil date: *"7 September (Julian), which falls
on 20 September 2026"*. Measured across the corpus, **every** venerated
attestation carries a feast — 0 of them without — so there is no Russian or
Serbian veneration this does not already cover, and saint.spec.js has pinned the
Julian and Revised Julian forms since Amendment 31.

What can look like the feature missing is an attestation whose status is
`undocumented`: Anthony's Serbian row prints no feast because the corpus has no
Serbian entry for him, which is the site declining to invent one rather than a
gap in the display. That distinction is worth keeping visible, and it is the
reason this was checked against a rendered page before anything was written.

### Two recorded, and neither acted on

* **The script-forms search question is closed with a number.** 742 saints carry
  a `names` array, 1,142 forms in all: **93,961 bytes raw, 20,606 gzipped** —
  about 4% on the 490 kB manifest, on the boot path. The author's decision is to
  record it and not act.

  **The trap beside it, for whoever reads either field cold: there are two
  things called `names` in this codebase.** A saint record's `names` is the
  saint's own name in other scripts. It is not the search index, and it is not
  `display_name`. A change to one is not a change to the other.

* **The Index's 72ch column is deferred, not declined.** The author's answer to
  breaking the Index out of it is *not now, because a separate desktop layout
  design may come later*. That is a different thing from a no on the merits, and
  it is written down that way on purpose: a reader who finds a bare "no" here
  stops asking, and this one is waiting on a larger piece of work.

### Macarie's dates: three sources, no resolution

The plate the author approved carries its own caption — "portarie al sfinteĭ
Mitropoliĭ din Bucurescĭ (1780 saŭ 1785—1845)" — while
`saints/macarius-the-protopsaltes/saint.json` records birth 1763 from
doxologia.ro, with no death, and the standard references are usually given as
1836. Three sets of dates for one man, and one of them is uncertain in its own
words.

**The record keeps 1763 and gains no death date.** Nothing here has been
checked against a source this project holds: a lithograph's caption is a claim,
not a citation, and "usually given as 1836" is a report of references rather
than a reading of one. The birth note is extended to say that the plate and the
standard references disagree, and with what — which is the same treatment every
other uncertain date in this corpus gets. Inventing a resolution between three
sources is precisely the invention Amendment 2 forbids, and a date this project
cannot source is a date it does not print.

## Amendment 62 — the ruler was wrong (2026-08-28, twenty-first sitting)

The last of the load-sensitive family, and the first that was not about timing
at all.

### A test that only passed in the wrong face

`a row prints its name whole and is only as tall as that name needs` had been
failing intermittently for a day, naming a **different saint each run** — the
signature of a text measurement rather than a race with a clock. The peer
session checked it against an earlier commit in a worktree rather than assuming,
and it failed there too, which ruled out that day's image batch.

The first fix was the obvious one and was right as far as it went: a row's
height is worked out from the name measured in the face resolved *at layout
time*, which on a cold load is the fallback, and `wireGrid`'s
`document.fonts.ready` hook re-lays the rows when the webfont lands. The site
repairs itself and the test was reading between the two states —
`await document.fonts.ready` in the page does not order a test after the app's
own `.then` on that same promise. So the window is polled until every row agrees
with its own line count.

**That was not the whole of it, and preloading the Latin subsets is what
exposed the rest.** With the face now arriving reliably (Amendment 61), the test
went from intermittent to red every single time, on this:

```js
clipped: name.scrollHeight > name.clientHeight + 1
```

Measured on a rendered page: a **one-line** name in a 21.25 px line box reports
`scrollHeight` 23 against `clientHeight` 21. Every row in Literata answers
"clipped". The names were never cut off — the ruler was wrong, and it had only
ever passed because the rows were being read before the webfont arrived.

Clipping is now measured against the clamp's own allowance, which is what the
word means: a name is cut off when three lines were not enough for it.

**The lesson is the uncomfortable one.** A green test told us the names were
whole; what it actually told us was that the font had not loaded. The fix for a
flake had to go through *making the flake worse* — the preload turned an
intermittent red into a permanent one — before the real fault was visible at
all. A test that passes only in a fallback face is not a weaker test, it is a
test of something else.

### Macarie's dates: recorded, not resolved

The record keeps birth 1763 from doxologia.ro and gains no death date. Two other
sets are in circulation and neither has been read against a source this project
holds: the lithograph's own caption, "portarie al sfintei Mitropolii din
Bucuresti (1780 sau 1785-1845)", which is uncertain in its own words; and
byzantion.ro, whose article title gives 1750-1836 **while reproducing that same
plate uncaptioned**, so the page disagrees with its own illustration.

The birth note says all of that. A caption is a claim rather than a citation, a
report of what references "usually give" is not a reading of one, and a date
this corpus cannot source is a date it does not print. Choosing between three
unsourced numbers is the invention Amendment 2 forbids; saying that three exist
is the honest alternative, and it is what the record now does.

### Two sessions, one machine

Worth writing down because it cost both of us runs and is nowhere in the
documents: **this repository is worked by two agent sessions at once, and they
share a port.** `playwright.config.js` refuses to reuse a server it did not
start, so a run started while another is live dies on "4173 is already used" —
and the reflex, killing whatever holds the port, kills the other session's
suite mid-flight. One gate here died at test 494 of 528 that way, with a 0 ms
failure and a truncated log, which reads like a broken test and is not one.
`Stop-Process -Name node -Force` is worse: it takes everything.

The rule that came out of it: **ask before you clear the port, and say when you
start a long run.** A dead run is cheap; a dead run misread as a red gate is
not, and both of us spent time on failures that belonged to the other's
uncommitted tree.

## Amendment 63 — the rehearsal did not reach half of its own test (2026-08-28, twenty-second sitting)

The loose end Amendment 62 handed over deliberately, and it turned out to be a
smaller fault than it looked and a symptom of a much larger one.

### What was actually wrong

`a row prints its name whole and is only as tall as that name needs` ends with a
block about the *desktop* column, and that block opens its own
`browser.newContext()` — a fresh context rather than a resize and a reload,
because the layout is a stored setting and a test that reloads is testing that
write's timing as much as anything it means to.

The COLD_FACE fixture decorates the **injected `page`**. A context the test opens
itself is a page that fixture never saw. So under `COLD_FACE=1` the first two
thirds of this test ran forced and the last third did not, and the last third is
the only text measurement in it about the desktop column.

**Measured rather than reasoned about**, by asking both pages what they had:

    [forced page] "Times New Roman", Times, serif   literata:false   column 295
    [fresh  ctx ] Literata, "Iowan Old Style", …    literata:true    column 678

That is the whole defect. It was never a red — the block's assertions are all
true in Literata, which is the face their numbers were written in.

### It was not failing, and that is the point

The handover said this block *fails* under the rehearsal. It does not, at
`f723798`: **24 of 24** repeats at both projects under `COLD_FACE=1`, and the
whole spec green. What it does is worse and quieter — it reports itself as a
rehearsal and exempts the one block that most needs one.

The rehearsal now reaches it: `coldFace(page)` is exported from e2e/fixtures.js
as the single implementation of the treatment, the fixture calls it, and so does
the test on the context it opens.

### The block holds in the forced face, and it is not the deal's luck

Whether it *could* be rehearsed was an open question, because the block asserts
that every row at 1280 is one line, and its page opens in **Random order with a
fresh seed** — the Amendment 57 trap, where an assertion is a property of the
deal. Twenty-four green repeats would not have settled it.

So every row in the corpus was swept at the desktop column, in both faces:

| | grid column | line available | longest name | rows on one line |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Literata (warm) | 678 px | 600 px | 536.1 px | **734 of 734** |
| Times New Roman (COLD_FACE) | 580 px | 502 px | 447.8 px | **734 of 734** |

(The line is the grid column less `ROW_TEXT_INSET`, which is 78; both grid
widths were read off the wide context itself rather than taken from the facet
row's proof line.)

The longest name is *Venerable Martyr Macarius the New, disciple of Patriarch
Niphon* in both. Both faces leave about 11% of the line unused, because the
narrower face is paid for by a narrower 72ch column — the two very nearly
cancel. **No deal can produce a wrapped row at this width in either face**, so
the block is not deal-dependent and needed no exclusion.

### The pin, and what a back-out of it looks like

A fix to a rehearsal has an awkward property: backing it out leaves every
assertion in the block **green**, because Literata is what the numbers were
written in. There is nothing to go red. So the block asks the page directly:

```js
if (COLD) {
  expect(
    await widePage.evaluate(() => document.fonts.check('1em Literata')),
    'the cold-face rehearsal did not reach the context this test opened itself',
  ).toBe(false);
}
```

Backed out — the `coldFace(widePage)` call removed — it fails by that name,
`Expected: false / Received: true`. Restored, green. It is conditional on `COLD`
on purpose: in the ordinary gate, asserting the webfont *did* arrive would be an
assertion about `font-display: optional`'s window rather than about this test.

This is the same instrument-honesty rule the fixture's own header states — a
rehearsal that silently failed to apply would also be green — applied to the
rehearsal one level down.

### The larger fault: 42 contexts, and a general fix that measured green while doing nothing

The suite opens **42 contexts of its own**, and 41 of them are still outside the
rehearsal. Closing them all looked like ten lines: wrap `browser.newContext`
inside the `page` fixture so every context the tests open is treated too.

It was written, and it came back **528 passed, 2 skipped, both projects, zero
failures** — and it had closed almost nothing. **36 of the suite's tests take
`{ browser }` and never ask for `page` at all**, so a patch that lives in the
`page` fixture never runs for precisely the tests that open the most contexts.
The green was the green of a change that had not happened.

It was caught by proving it bit rather than by reading the result: with the
per-test call removed *and* the wrap in place the pin still passed, which said
the wrap worked — for that test, which takes `{ page }`. Counting the signatures
is what said it worked for almost nothing else.

**It is not committed.** Closing the other 41 wants a worker-scoped `browser`
override and a pin inside a `{ browser }` test to prove it bit, and it tightens
41 tests' constraints at once against a rehearsal that is deliberately harsher
than the runner — Verdana is wider than DejaVu and Times narrower than the
runner's serif. That is its own sitting. The dead end is written into
`coldFace`'s own doc comment so the next person does not spend the run finding
it again.

### Verification

174 unit. **530 browser** across both projects, Playwright exit 0, no `failed`,
`flaky` or `✘` line anywhere in the log. The rehearsal run separately —
`COLD_FACE=1 npx playwright test`, both projects — **528 passed, 2 skipped**,
exit 0, with the harness's own proof lines printing on both projects. The test
itself at a **rate** rather than a green: 24 of 24 forced and 24 of 24 warm,
twelve repeats at each project, before and after.

## Amendment 64 — a count nobody could audit (2026-08-28, twenty-third sitting)

The handover said to re-measure before acting on "19 day-leaders have no icon",
and predicted the answer was **at most 18**: the count predated that day's image
work, Macarie had been one of them and now has a portrait. Both halves of that
turned out to be wrong, and the way they were wrong is the point.

### The measurement

The app's own path, not a re-implementation: `buildFeastIndex`, `entriesInChurch`
and `pickHero`, over `data/manifest.json`. For every (day, church) pair with at
least one entry, pick the hero the page would pick and ask whether the manifest
gives him an image.

**Over calendar year 2026 — 133 day-and-church combinations carrying an entry:**

| | imageless leads | distinct saints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| without the sung-and-imaged tie-break | 37 | 32 |
| **with it (what ships)** | **26** | **21** |

Not 19, and not 18. The corpus is **130 saints with an icon**, not the 128
HANDOFF carried.

### The denominator was a phrase

The first pass came back **266** combinations, which is exactly twice 133: the
feast index maps a stored feast onto *every* year, so building it for 2026 and
2027 counts every saint twice — and because `pickHero` hashes the ISO date, the
two years pick *different* heroes and the duplicates do not even collapse.

Amendment 59 said "measured over the days the four calendars cover". That is not
a population anyone can reconstruct. Sweeping candidate ranges found the one that
gives 133: it is **the whole of calendar year 2026**, not the day-record range
(that is 115) and not the corpus's own reach (112). **A count whose denominator
is a phrase cannot be audited, including by the person who wrote it.** Both this
amendment and `pickHero`'s comment now name the population with the number.

### 19 was never right, and the argument said so before the check did

Something was wrong before any commit was consulted. **Adding an icon can only
ever lower this count.** Give a saint a picture and either he is in the day's
sung pool, in which case `sungImaged` becomes non-empty and the day now leads
with an image; or he is not, and the pool is untouched. There is no path by
which a day that led with an imaged saint starts leading with an imageless one.
So 19 rising to 21 cannot be an effect of the new icons, and the two numbers had
to be counting different things.

`data/manifest.json` is generated and gitignored, so the check is a worktree at
`b11322c` — Amendment 59's own commit — and `npm run build:manifest` there. At
that commit, over that population:

* **133 combinations — reproduces exactly.**
* **27 imageless leads — reproduces exactly.**
* **22 distinct saints — the amendment says 19.**

Two of three numbers coming back to the digit is what says the method is the
same one; the third is a miscount. Macarie's portrait then closed exactly one
day, 27 to 26 and 22 to 21, which is the whole of that day's effect on this
figure.

### The prediction in the handover was worse than the count it corrected

"At most 18" was inference — one icon subtracted from a remembered base — and it
was carried across a handover in the same register as the measured facts beside
it. It was wrong twice over: the base was 22 rather than 19, and subtracting was
the wrong operation to be confident about anyway.

**A predicted count deserves the same distrust as a remembered one.** The
handover was right to say "re-measure before acting"; what it should not have
done is say what the answer would be. This one cost nothing because it was
checked. The value of writing it down is that the next session reads a number in
a briefing and asks whose measurement it was.

### Three entries in "needs the author" had already been answered

Checked against the tree rather than against the prose, and **marked closed in
place with the commit that closed each**, because a deleted entry loses the
trail:

* **Athanasius reads *Confessor*** — closed at Amendment 60 (`10fbb5a`). His
  types are `bishop, theologian`. The reasoning is kept because it is still live
  for the seven records deliberately left standing, and those were re-counted:
  **exactly 7, and exactly the seven named** — Barses and Eulogius of Edessa,
  Liberius of Rome, Martin the Pope, Nicholas of Alma-Ata, Paul the New of
  Constantinople, Protogenes of Carrhae.
* **Seven image source links** — closed at `6905aba`. **Zero** `example.invalid`
  left under `saints/`, and the build warnings with them.
* **Font preload** — built at Amendment 61 (`7eea8f8`). What is still owed is not
  the work but a **second pair of eyes**: `7eea8f8` is the one commit in this
  stretch marked verified by its author only, and that is now said in the entry
  rather than left in a provenance list somebody has to cross-reference.

### Verification

No behaviour changed — the only source edit is `pickHero`'s comment. 174 unit,
530 browser across both projects, Playwright exit 0, no `failed`, `flaky` or `✘`
line in the log. The audit script is `.tmp/leaders-audit.mjs`, untracked, and
every figure above was printed by it rather than reasoned to.

## Amendment 65 — five red runs nobody had looked at (2026-08-28, twenty-fourth sitting)

The verifying session went to check whether CI was green for what had been
pushed. It was not, and it had not been for five pushes.

    b11322c  success        <- last green, and what the live site was serving
    6905aba  failure        the licence test, both projects
    f4dc423  failure        the die, and `a row prints its name whole`
    f723798  failure        the die (+ the rail's coast, flaky, retried green)
    da5f457  failure        the die, both projects, 528 passed
    223c203  failure        the die, both projects, 528 passed

**The deploy job is gated on the build job, so it was skipped every time.** The
site had been frozen at `b11322c` for the whole of the work above it, including
three commits whose subject was verification.

Two of the three failures were already closed — `f4dc423` fixed the licence
test and `f723798` fixed the row-name test, each after the run that caught it.
The third was live and is fixed here.

### The die is not square on the runner, and the fault is a token

    the die is square … Error: die 30.265625 x 31.265625

`--facet-h` is arithmetic: `font-size x line-height + padding + 2`. A chip left
to size itself is a **line box**, which is that plus whatever the face's own
ascent and descent add. The two agree to the pixel on a Windows desk and differ
by one on the runner, whose `system-ui` is DejaVu Sans. The die takes its width
from the token and its height from the flex line, so where those disagree it is
a pixel taller than it is wide.

Both of the author's instructions are involved and they had been in silent
tension since 2026-08-26: *"make the dice button square proportions … as wide as
it is tall"* and *"make the dice button height match the height of the other
filters in its row"*. On a face whose line box exceeds the token, only one can
hold — unless something pins the row.

**Four candidates were measured rather than argued about**, against the fault
forced on this desk:

| | die | chip | square | matches row |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| as shipped | 30.27 x 34.27 | 34.27 | no | yes |
| `aspect-ratio` on the die | 30.27 x 34.27 | 34.27 | **no** | yes |
| …with `min-height: 0` | 23 x 34.27 | 34.27 | no | yes |
| drop the stretch | 30.27 x 30.27 | 34.27 | yes | **no** |
| **pin the chip to `--facet-h`** | **30.27 x 30.27** | **30.27** | **yes** | **yes** |

`aspect-ratio` does nothing here, which is worth knowing: **Chromium will not
transfer a *stretched* cross size to the main size.** The width it produced was
the transfer of `min-height`, not of the height the row actually gave — which is
why removing `min-height` collapsed it to its content at 23 px rather than
squaring it.

So the chip is pinned: `height: var(--facet-h)` on `.facet > summary`, which
reaches the filter chips and the foot's Sort and View alike. **The token already
claimed to be "the chips' own height"; this makes the claim true** rather than
an estimate that happens to be right on one platform. A face that wants another
pixel now centres its text in the same box instead of growing the row under a
control that cannot follow it.

### The test forces the condition through the chip's *content*

The first version forced it through the chip's *box* — 2 px of extra block
padding — and reproduced the runner's failure exactly, 30.27 by 34.27 on both
projects. Then the fix made **the forcing stop working** rather than making the
assertion pass: with the height pinned, extra padding no longer grows the chip,
so the premise assertion fired instead.

That is the third appearance in two sittings of one fault — *a check that cannot
tell "fixed" from "the check fell off"* — and the second where a premise saved
it. The forcing is a bigger **font** now: `--facet-h` is computed from
`--facet-font` on `:root` and is untouched by a font-size on the chip, exactly
as the token is untouched by DejaVu being taller than Segoe UI. Content wants
more room; whether the box grows is the question under test.

The premise moved too, for the same reason. "The chip's content overflows its
box" is only true *after* the fix, so backing the fix out failed there — on a
message that reads like the harness slipping. It asserts the forcing *landed*
(computed font-size is 20px), which holds in both states, and the back-out now
fails where it should: `the chip grew from 30.265625 to 41, which is what leaves
the die behind`.

### `COLD_FACE` does not reach this, and that bounds what it is for

Measured by the verifying session, warm and forced, both green: **the rehearsal
does not reproduce the one failure that was actually red on the runner.** It
forces a font *family*, which decides where text wraps. The die's fault is how
tall a line box is, and that is a *metrics* question — DejaVu's ascent and
descent are not Verdana's.

So `COLD_FACE` is a **wrapping** instrument, not a leading one. Whether other
line-height-dependent assertions share the blind spot is a question and not a
finding; what is settled is that "green under COLD_FACE" is not "CI-safe".

### A red run left no evidence

The workflow has always uploaded `playwright-report/` on failure. Nothing ever
wrote it: `playwright.config.js` set the CI reporter to `[github, list]` with no
`html`. Every red run warned `No files were found with the provided path` and
uploaded nothing, so the only way to see any of this was the raw job log through
the API. Fixed here, and verified by running with `CI=1` and watching
`playwright-report/index.html` appear.

**A gate whose failures cannot be read is a gate people stop reading**, and five
pushes is how long that took.

### And the rehearsal turned up a flake that is not this sitting's

The full `COLD_FACE` run came back red on a third test — `the carousel fades in
rather than appearing, and comes back where it was left`. The suspicion was that
pinning the chips had shortened the controls row under the forced face and moved
a remembered scroll.

**It had not.** At `--repeat-each=12 --workers=10` under `COLD_FACE=1` it failed
10 of 24 with the fix in and **7 of 24 with this sitting's changes stashed** —
the control run, done that way so the number could not be blamed on the change
it was being used to clear. A pre-existing, contention-sensitive flake: at the
default worker count a single rehearsal run passes often enough that four of
them in this sitting alone came back green.

**It is not fixed here**, and that is a scoping decision rather than an
oversight: the site has been undeployed for five pushes and the die is what
unblocks it. It is written into HANDOFF as the next thing to take, with its
rate and its control, because Amendment 60's rule says a flake in the rehearsal
costs more than a flake in the gate — that run is the only local instrument that
predicts the runner.

### Verification

174 unit; the full browser suite at both projects; the rehearsal separately. The
fix backed out in **both halves separately** and confirmed red on the symptom
rather than on the premise, and the neighbouring `the die is a chip height,
including on a line of its own` — the 2026-08-26 case the stretch was added
for, and the one the obvious fix reintroduces — green throughout.

**Say which back-out, because two are possible and they prove different
things** (corrected after the verifying session ran the other one). Removing the
chip's `height` and running warm gives `the chip grew from 30.265625 to 41`.
For the die, *restoring `align-self: stretch` and `min-height` in place of the
height* is the back-out that demonstrates the claim — `die 30.265625 x 31.6875`
under `COLD_FACE=1`, which is pinning-beats-stretching. Merely *deleting* the
die's height leaves it nothing to take a height from at all and gives
`die 30.265625 x 23`, which is the 2026-08-26 collapse rather than this
amendment's case. Both are red, so the declaration is load-bearing either way;
only the first is evidence for what is claimed here. Rendered at 1280 and 360 and
looked at: the die is a circle on the chips' own line, nothing clipped.

**None of that is a green CI run**, which is the whole subject of this
amendment. What this sitting can honestly claim is a local gate and a diagnosis;
the Actions run on the commit is the evidence, and it is owed before the next
thing is built on top.

## Amendment 66 — a millisecond budget standing in for a state, twice more (2026-08-28, twenty-fifth sitting)

Amendment 65 recorded three live flakes rather than fixing them, because the
site had been undeployed for five pushes and the die was what unblocked it. CI
went green on `4f971d7` and **the deploy job ran for the first time since
`b11322c`**, so these are the next thing.

Two are closed. Both were the same fault, and it is the one Amendment 60 named:
**the assertion is almost never the problem.**

### The same shape twice

| test | window | what it reported |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `the carousel fades in rather than appearing` | 1500 ms | `the carousel never came back` |
| `the die stays while the page goes` | 1600 ms | `the roll never landed on a saint` |

Each traces an animation inside the page and stops at a fixed number of
milliseconds. Under contention the thing being watched takes longer than the
window, the trace ends mid-flight, and what the test reports is an **absence** —
which reads exactly like the feature being broken. Both poll to the arrival now,
with a ceiling well past any real duration, so a loaded machine takes longer
rather than going red.

### The carousel had a second cause, and it was the real one

Fixing the window took it from 7 of 24 to **4 of 24**, which is the useful kind
of partial result: it says the remaining failures are something else.

They were, and the numbers named it. Every failing run had read its own seed back
as a bare **2400** — the exact value the test writes — while every passing run
read **4374** or **5165**. A seed that comes back unchanged means it landed on a
track sitting at 0.

`loopScroll` re-measures from its own frame until the geometry is real and only
then applies the clone buffer's offset; until that happens the track is at 0 and
**a `scrollLeft` written into it is discarded when the loop finally measures**.
The row then opens wherever the buffer puts it — 2752, or 1965 — and the test
reports a restore that never failed. CLAUDE.md has warned since 2026-08-27 that
this loop is not measurable until it says so; the test predated the warning.

Waiting for the track to be past 0 — the buffer's own offset, and never zero —
took the remainder out.

**Three candidate diagnoses were wrong before this one was right**, and each was
discarded by measurement rather than by argument: that the window was the whole
of it (instrumented: every run collected 57 to 68 samples, so the window was not
even reached); that pinning the chips at Amendment 65 had moved a remembered
scroll (control on a stashed tree: 7 of 24 either way); and that the run was
being rebuilt between the two switches, dropping the offset by design
(`runChanged: false` and identical `scrollWidth` on every failure). **The trace
that settled it was not of the failure but of the seed**, which is the one value
both good and bad runs report differently.

### Rates, before and after

| test | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `the carousel fades in` | 7 of 24 | **0 of 24** |
| `the die stays while the page goes` | 10 of 24, 4 of 24 on a quieter machine | **0 of 24** |

`--repeat-each=12 --workers=10`, the carousel's under `COLD_FACE=1` and the
roll's warm; each fix **backed out against the rate** and confirmed to bring the
failures back. The roll's two before-figures are the same code on the same desk
at different loads, which is worth keeping visible: a flake rate is a
measurement of the machine as much as of the test, and quoting one without its
conditions is how "the suite has no known flakes" got written.

### What is left

The rail's coast, which went flaky **on CI** at `f723798` and retried green. It
has never been reproduced here — 148 contended runs at Amendment 60, none since
— so it is the one flake whose rate this desk cannot measure, and it stays
recorded rather than guessed at.

### Verification

174 unit; the full browser suite at both projects; the rehearsal separately.
Both fixes backed out against a rate. No source file was touched: this is two
tests learning to wait, and the product paths they watch are unchanged.

## Amendment 67 — the throttle reproduces what the load could not (2026-08-28, twenty-sixth sitting)

The rail's coast is this suite's oldest flake. Amendment 60 fixed the gesture,
proved it against **148 contended runs with none failing**, and the entry has
read as closed since. It is not closed, and the verifying session's reading of
the Actions API is what said so:

    f723798   flaky, BOTH projects
    09ad096   desktop FAILED THROUGH THE RETRY; mobile flaky
    102fd83   desktop, flaky

**Three of the ten runs since the spec split**, and one of them was two
consecutive failures in one job — with `retries: 1`, a red gate that only the
die's own red was hiding.

### 148 runs said nothing because contention was the wrong instrument

The thing this desk could never do was make the gesture slow. Parallel load
makes *round trips* slow, and Amendment 60 had already moved the gesture inside
the page precisely to take round trips out of it.

CDP does it in one line — `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate` — and the gesture's
own span answers immediately:

| throttle | span of the four moves | coasts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1x | 25 ms | yes |
| 6x | 33 ms | yes |
| 20x | 81 ms | yes |
| **150x** | **140 ms** | **no** |

And the shape is right: at 150x it is the **first** gesture that spans 140 ms
while every one after it spans 26 ms. This test runs once, cold, per CI job.

### A spin bounds the gap from below, not from above

`throwRail` spaces its four moves with `spin(8)` — a busy-wait on
`performance.now()`, chosen at Amendment 60 because a spin blocks and the
spacing is therefore real elapsed time. True, and it guarantees **at least**
8 ms. It guarantees nothing at the top.

The rail prunes its samples at 80 ms per move (`hold.samples`) and again at
120 ms on release (`fresh`). Stretch the gesture past those and the fresh
samples collapse, the velocity is computed over nothing, and the rail settles —
correctly. **The rail was never wrong. The test reported "did not coast" when
what happened was that nobody threw it**, and that mistranslation is the whole
history of this test: Amendment 60 diagnosed exactly this fault, fixed the
round-trip half of it, and left the machine-speed half standing.

### Measured, then re-thrown, then asserted

`throwRail` now times its own gesture and throws again if the span exceeds
60 ms — up to eight attempts, all inside one `evaluate`, with a fresh
`pointerdown` cancelling any coast a slow attempt started. **The product path is
untouched.** It returns `{ released, span, attempts, delivered }`, and both
callers assert `delivered` **before** asserting anything about the rail:

```
could not deliver a flick in 8 attempts; best span 355.9 ms
```

That is the test saying which of the two things went wrong, which it has never
been able to do.

### Verified against the throttle, in both directions

| | at 150x |
| --- | --- |
| with the retry | **6 of 6 delivered**, 1 to 4 attempts each, coast every time |
| one attempt only | **5 of 8 not a flick** (spans 75 to 356 ms); the coast itself failed 1 of 8 |

Worth reading precisely: with a single attempt the gesture usually fails to be a
flick and the rail *still* coasts, because the pruned velocity often clears
`MIN_FLICK` anyway. The test only goes red at the tail. **That is why the rate
looks small from either end and why it survived 148 runs** — and it is the
argument for asserting the premise rather than the rate, because the premise
fails five times more often than the test does and says so plainly.

### What this does not claim

**It does not claim the CI flake is closed.** What is demonstrated is a
mechanism, reproduced locally and fixed against the instrument that reproduces
it. Whether it is *the* mechanism on the runner is a question only the next ten
Actions runs answer, and the entry in HANDOFF says so with its SHAs so that a
successor checks rather than assumes.

Two things recorded beside it and neither acted on. **4 of the 5 sightings are
desktop**, which is the opposite of where this suite's faults usually live — at
n=5 an observation, not a finding, and worth a thought before the gesture is
blamed a second time. And `random deals an order, and holds it still under the
reader` has now been seen **twice in about thirty runs**, `fbcaef8` and
`102fd83`; it was reported as non-recurring after the first and recurred, which
is the kind of sentence that should not be left standing.

### Replicated, and the instrument has a trap of its own

The verifying session reproduced all of this independently, and took two
attempts — which is the useful part. Its first probe set the throttle, *then*
navigated: eight runs, spans 26 to 35 ms, delivered and coasting every time. On
its own that reads as "the mechanism does not reproduce", and it was nearly
reported that way.

**A throttle applied before a navigation does not survive it.** Timed twice on
this desk, once by each session, with a fixed 3e6-iteration loop in the page:
the ratio is **3.8x** when the rate is set before the `goto` and **35x** when it
is set after. *Twice on one desk, not on two machines* — the distinction is
`ac7db1a`'s own house rule, written four commits earlier and nearly contradicted
here in the file sessions read first. What a second run rules out is a
transcription slip, not a machine-specific result; this trap happens to be
deterministic, and reproduced first time in both sessions. With it
verifiably biting, 4 of 6 single-attempt gestures were not flicks — and the two
that were are the two runs where the ratio said the throttle had stopped biting
at that moment. **The gesture fails exactly when the page is slow and not
otherwise**, which is a tighter correlation than the rate alone gives. With the
default eight tries, every run delivered in **one attempt at 26 to 27 ms**.

Note also that the achieved ratio is not the requested one: 150 was asked for
and 21x to 135x was measured — and those figures and the 35x above are **the
same machine under different load**, which is the sharper reason to print the
ratio. A throttle rate is not merely a request rather than a setting; the
slowdown it buys is not stable within one desk, so a number taken from it is
only worth what the run that printed it says.

And the peer's four undelivered gestures **all still coasted**, matching the
back-out here: the test would have passed with its premise false. That is the
argument for asserting `delivered` first, from the other end.

**This is the third instrument in this repo to fail by looking like a pass** —
after the `COLD_FACE` fixture that never reached a self-made context and the
preload that shipped one subset twice. In all three the silent no-op and the
success are the same green, and the defence is the same: make the instrument
report what it did. HANDOFF carries that as a class now rather than as three
anecdotes.

### The fix did not close it, and the failure is not a flake

CI on `90600f5` came back flaky on the same test, and on `1f9069e` **red through
the retry**, with the deploy skipped. The numbers are the finding:

    90600f5 (flaky)     Expected > 4388   Received 4345
    1f9069e attempt 1   Expected > 4388   Received 4345
    1f9069e retry #1    Expected > 4388   Received 4345

**Identical to the pixel, three attempts across two runs**, with `released` 4368
every time. Timing noise scatters; this does not. It is a deterministic state
the runner sometimes enters, and what varies is whether it is entered at all.

**The `delivered` assertion passed on all three.** The gesture was a flick; the
harness did its job. So the throttle mechanism of this amendment is real *and*
excluded as the cause of these three, which is what a premise assertion is for —
before it, this run would have said "the rail did not coast" and told nobody
whether it had been thrown.

### What was measured next, and why nothing shipped for it

Locally, with the gesture now reliable, the rail was found to **rebuild its own
window mid-coast**: the strip's first day moved from 2026-06-29 to 2026-08-21
and `scrollLeft` reset from 7995 to a canonical 4489. A coast that carries the
cursor near the edge of the loaded range re-anchors, and *position after a
re-anchor measures nothing the reader would notice*. CI's "23 px backwards" is
plausibly the same event seen small.

So the test was rewritten to watch `is-coasting` — the instrument Amendment 60
established for this rail's absence case — instead of inferring a coast from net
displacement. It passed, and **it was not shipped**, because at
`--repeat-each=12 --workers=10` it failed **5 of 48** on a different assertion:
`state.aligned`, deterministically, at `released at 4287`. The old test never
reached that line because it failed earlier. **A second fault sits behind the
first**, and "at rest" detected as two equal reads 100 ms apart can be a pause
inside a sequence rather than the end of one.

**That work is reverted and recorded rather than shipped**, on the verifying
session's advice and on the day's own evidence.

### The trace, read — and two more diagnoses killed by it

`1f9069e`'s retry recorded one. It does **not** carry a scrollLeft timeline
(frame snapshots do not record scroll, and poll results are not stored), but it
carries the action list and 26 screencast frames, and both are decisive.

**The rebuild hypothesis is wrong.** At the moment of failure the rail's window
is the canonical one — 121 buttons, first Monday 29 June 2026, last Tuesday 27
October, 2026-08-28 at index 60, dead centre. Nothing re-anchored. The local
reproduction was a real behaviour of the rail and **not** what CI hit.

**There was no coast.** The screencast records only visual change, and after the
throw at 969 ms there are exactly **two frames — 1115 ms and 1128 ms — and then
nothing for the remaining four seconds**. Read side by side they show the rail
one column further on and then moving *backwards*: a drag of 100 px, a release,
and a settle pulling back to alignment. The action list agrees; the nine
`.week-strip` resolutions from 1039 ms to 5085 ms at doubling intervals are the
failing poll and nothing else happened between them.

**`prefers-reduced-motion` was the next hypothesis and it is also wrong.**
`beginCoast` is guarded by `!reducedMotion()`, and a context forced to `reduce`
gives net **0 px** from the release against **+272** under `no-preference` —
the right shape. But pinning the test to `no-preference` and then backing it out
to `reduce` **left the test passing**, because the settle alone can carry more
than the 20 px the assertion asks for depending on where the release lands. A
fix whose back-out does not fail is pinning nothing, so it was not shipped
either.

**Five diagnoses of this test have now been killed by measurement in one day**:
the sampling window, the chip pin, the run being rebuilt, the rail re-anchoring,
and reduced motion. What is established is narrow and worth having — on CI the
gesture is delivered, no coast runs, and the rail settles backwards by 23 px,
deterministically. Why no coast runs when the velocity should clear `MIN_FLICK`
is the open question, and it is the rail's own arithmetic. **The next person
should instrument the rail rather than the test**: log the fresh-sample count
and the computed velocity at release behind a flag, push it, and read the CI
console. Nothing this desk can run has reproduced it.

### Verification

174 unit; the full browser suite at both projects; the rehearsal separately. The
fix verified against the CPU throttle rather than against a green — 6 of 6 with
it, and the single-attempt back-out failing to deliver a flick 5 of 8 with the
coast itself red 1 of 8. No source file touched: this is the harness learning
whether it did what it said.
